source.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
source.authors: Min-Jun Zhu; Lin-Yi Yang; Yifan Wei; Ning-Yu Zhang; Yue Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present and not cut off. Some figure text is garbled in the supplied extraction; the relevant prose and Table 1/Table 2 values are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper fine-tunes aligned chat models on harmful and benign data and evaluates harmful-output behavior, directly applying the fine-tuning intervention and safety evaluation relevant to the original claim, though with different datasets and experimental details.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure per-token KL across response positions, compliant-token prefilling, or decoding changes. It does test GCG, an adversarial-suffix attack, on a fine-tuned model. Values used to select safety-sensitive heads are not recorded as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The paper fine-tunes aligned Llama-3-8B/70B-Instruct and Mistral-Large-2 on explicitly harmful data (HH-RLHF negatives), Qi et al.'s 10 identity-shifting examples, and 50k Alpaca samples. It reports harmful compliance on HEx-PHI using the original GPT-4 1–5 judge and harmfulness rate, plus AdvBench ASR. These are the original method and measure. However, the paper's purpose is the SafetyLock mitigation, and Table 1 gives no unfine-tuned baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that SafetyLock, an inference-time head-steering method using directions taken from the original model, restores safety in fine-tuned models at all three risk levels and against prompt attacks, with little loss of capability. That harmful, identity-shifting and benign fine-tuning compromise safety is presented as the motivating threat. They also conclude that fine-tuned models retain the original model's safety activation directions.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes aligned chat models on explicitly harmful HH-RLHF negative samples and Alpaca data, then evaluates HEx-PHI harmfulness and AdvBench ASR. The paper cites the original fine-tuning vulnerability work but uses its own datasets, models, and setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences across model, fine-tuning risk level, training sample count, intervention strength α, intervention degree K, and attack method. For GCG, reported attack outcomes also vary substantially by defense.

fits_no_version.finding: After fine-tuning at all risk levels, the safe-versus-unsafe activation direction in a top head (L31 H26, Llama-3-8B) is preserved: KL below 1e-5 versus the original. Harmful compliance nonetheless rises.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning breaks safe behaviour while leaving safety-related representations largely intact, so the erosion is behavioural or shallow rather than a loss of the safety concept.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering only 6 of the top probe-selected attention heads cuts Llama-3-8B's harmfulness rate on the fine-tuned model from about 70% to about 15% (Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety after fine-tuning can be restored through activations in a small set of attention heads. This is steering, not weight localization.

record.problems: Table 1 does not state the harmful-example count associated with its Risk 1 values and gives no unfine-tuned comparison baseline. Harmfulness scores/rates and AdvBench ASR are not direct refusal-rate measurements. Several detailed plots have garbled text in the supplied extraction.
record.rows_left_out: The additional paired SafetyLock values in Table 1 are mitigation outcomes, not separate tests of the fine-tuning effects in V1/V2. Table 2 results for AutoDAN, DeepInception, and PAIR were not extracted because the claim version tested here concerns suffix attacks; GCG is the listed adversarial-suffix test. The paper's α and K sweeps were not extracted because they test the SafetyLock intervention rather than whether safety is localized in weights/ranks or shallow across tokens.

untested.parts: Dose–response at few-to-hundreds harmful examples. The 10/100/1000 conditions are only in an unreadable figure, and Table 1 does not state its sample count.
Benign datasets other than Alpaca (50k samples); there is no unfine-tuned baseline.
No per-token KL across response positions.
No prefilling or decoding attacks, and no suffix attack on the unfine-tuned aligned model. GCG on the fine-tuned model cannot isolate the bypass.
Weight or rank localization is not tested. Head selection serves the steering method only.
No training that deepens alignment; SafetyLock is an inference-time activation intervention.

missing.what: Risk 2 identity-shifting (10 Qi et al. AOA examples) results. Llama-3-8B: 3.19 / 53.33% / 38.46%; 70B: 2.12 / 15.63% / 9.42%; Mistral-Large-2: 4.79 / 92.12% / 82.50% (Score / Rate / ASR).
missing.versions: V2 (benign-looking identity data; V1 if implicit harm is classed as harmful)

missing.what: Unprotected ASR at 10, 100 and 1000 harmful examples (the sample-count sweep)
Per-category HEx-PHI harmfulness for Vanilla fine-tuned models

record.verdict_notes: The study is a mitigation paper. Its Vanilla numbers are the only evidence on the claim, and Table 1 lacks an unfine-tuned baseline and the Risk 1 sample count. The GCG rows (Table 2) are a defense comparison on an unspecified fine-tuned model and do not test V4. The record's V4 labels were removed, as was the V1 limits_scope label on r19 (10k examples is outside V1's range, not a failure). The tranche could arguably be T3, given new models and data, but the HEx-PHI GPT-4 judge and the AOA identity data follow the original.

versions.untested_parts: The reported tests do not establish that refusal is removed almost entirely. Table 1 does not state which harmful-training sample count its Risk 1 values use; the text separately reports a 10,000-example result.
Tests benign Alpaca fine-tuning, but does not report the same result for other ordinary or carefully chosen benign datasets. Table 1 does not give an unfine-tuned baseline.
No per-token KL measurement across response positions.
Tests GCG attacks, not compliant-start prefilling or decoding changes. The paper does not analyze whether an attack succeeds by getting past the first response tokens.
The paper selects attention heads for an inference-time intervention, but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
SafetyLock intervenes at inference time; the paper does not train safety to be deeper or test whether deepening holds up.
